title: How I Edited My Iceland Travel Film (Start to Finish)
creator: Jonah Pike
description:
Shooting tips, the edit, and the color grade for my 3-minute Iceland film.

Thanks to Framecut for sponsoring the editing section of this video.

Gear: one mirrorless body, a 24-70, a cheap ND filter, and a lot of hand warmers.

sentences.t: A lot of you asked how I made the little Iceland film I posted last month, so today I'm breaking down the whole process, from shooting to export.
And I want to be upfront, this was shot on one camera, one lens, by one very cold person.
Let's start with the shooting, because no edit can save footage you didn't get.
The first rule I gave myself was, every shot has to move.
Either the camera moves, or something in the frame moves, like waves, steam, a bird, my friend's ridiculous orange hat.
Static shots of landscapes look amazing in person and incredibly boring on a screen.
The second rule was, shoot the same thing three ways, wide, medium, and close.
So for the black sand beach, I've got the wide shot of the whole coastline, a medium of the waves hitting the rocks, and a close-up of the foam on the sand.
That gives you options in the edit, and it's the secret behind that cut-cut-cut rhythm you see in travel films.
And the third rule, record way more ambient sound than you think you need.
Wind, gravel crunching, the hiss of a hot spring, those sounds are half the feeling of the film.
Okay, so I came home with about four hours of footage for a three minute video.
This is where I jump into the edit, and Framecut is sponsoring this part of the video, so thank you to them.
I've got all my clips dropped into a new Framecut project, and the first thing I do is let it sort them by scene.
It groups the beach shots together, the waterfall shots together, and the driving shots together, which already saves me an hour of scrubbing.
Now I'm building the rough cut on the timeline, and I'm doing it to the music first, so I find the beat and just tap the M key on every downbeat to drop markers.
Then I drag clips onto the timeline and they snap right to those markers, which is how I get the cuts landing on the beat.
For the waterfall section, I want a speed ramp, so I select the clip, open the speed curve, and drag the middle down to about twenty percent.
See how the water slows down right as the music drops, and then snaps back to normal speed.
Next I'm layering the ambient sound underneath, so the wind track goes on its own audio lane, and I pull the volume down until you feel it more than hear it.
The last thing I do in here is color.
I put one adjustment layer over the whole timeline, add a little contrast, cool the shadows, and warm the highlights, so everything feels like the same trip.
Then I go clip by clip and match the exposure, because Iceland changes from bright sun to fog in about forty seconds.
Okay, so that's the edit, and here's what I learned from it.
The film got so much better when I cut the shots I loved but that didn't fit.
I had this gorgeous long shot of a glacier lagoon, and it slowed everything down, so it's gone, and it hurt.
The other big lesson is that the sound design carried way more of the emotion than the visuals did.
People keep telling me the film felt cold, and honestly that's the wind track, not the footage.
If I did it again, I'd shoot more of the people, because the shots of my friends laughing in the car are the ones everyone remembers.
Landscapes are beautiful, but people are the story.
If you've got questions about any of this, drop them below, I'll answer as many as I can.
And next time, I'm doing the same breakdown for a city, which is a completely different challenge.
See you then.
